A key aspect of our work has been educating 410 full-time university students in applied SiC and GaN power technology, while simultaneously facilitating internships and other university-industry collaborations. PowerAmerica has also made significant contributions in workforce training — engaging more than 3500 attendees through tutorials, short courses, and webinars. Finally, PowerAmerica has created course modules, teaching labs, test beds, and university courses that will make a lasting WBG educational impact. From 2015-2021, the timeframe summarized in this report, we performed 196 power SiC and GaN projects — which addressed chip design, fabrication, testing, modules, reliability, ruggedness, and circuit insertion in most major applications, including automotive and rail traction, on-board chargers, photovoltaic, consumer electronics, aerospace, flexible alternating current transmission systems (FACTS), high-voltage DC systems (HVDC), microgrids, energy storage, wind power, motor drives, UPS, and data centers. Execution of these seed projects demonstrated SiC and GaN competitive system advantages — and their outcomes led to the launch of numerous commercial products. Moreover, in turn, the success of PowerAmerica’s projects drove industry investment in WBG technologies — creating high-tech manufacturing jobs and significant energy savings (reductions in CO2 emissions), which are crucial to the U.S. economy, national security, and the environment. 9 BP1 SYNOPSIS The first year of operation laid the groundwork for a successful, sustainable Institute driven by industry’s needs. A new facility was identified on NC State University’s Centennial Campus, and outfitted to meet the needs of the staff and members for special events. Staff was hired and the required business processes and operating systems were quickly put in place. Key hires included the Executive Director, Gen. Nick Justice and Deputy Director, John Muth. The communication, information security, IP management, and project management infrastructure were established to ensure industry proprietary information is protected, while channels for dialog and communication are available. The Institute received generous legal, administrative, and programmatic support from the NC State Office of Research and Innovation during this time. There was a heavy burden of administrative and operational requirements from DoE and this institutional support was invaluable. Once established, the team set to work to carry out the research agenda and the education program. Five focus areas were established to organize all activities and theses have remained in place for the life of the Institute: Focus Area 1 Management, Finance, and Operations Focus Area 2 Foundry and Device Development Focus Area 3 Module Manufacturing and Reliability Focus Area 4 Commercialization Applications Focus Area 5 Education and Workforce Development The first Call for Projects was released during BP1. This is the open, competitive solicitation for new projects, requiring cost share and membership that would be the main avenue for identifying and selecting the technical and education projects for funding throughout the life of the Institute. A secure, robust system was put in place to receive proposals, recruit independent external evaluators to review and score proposals, and award projects that met all the relevant criteria.
